answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-2: many owners of eligible cars value the rebate above their car and the cost of buying sooner (1.1 million eligible cars against V$4,000).

question.text: Will many of those eligible claim the payment, because it is worth more to them than what they must do or give up to qualify?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-1: sellers do not capture the whole rebate; some 30 competing brands; the rebate is shown on the invoice.

question.text: Will the recipients keep part of the payment, rather than sellers raising their prices by the whole of it?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-2 with SB-2's premise: buyers who take the rebate buy a new car they would not have bought in the window.

question.text: Will more of the subsidized good change hands than without the payment (because buyers buy more, or sellers can supply more)?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-7: the supply of eligible models cannot grow much within six months (shipping lead times of three to five months).

question.text: Is the sellers' supply of the subsidized good fixed for a while (stock ordered or built before the payment, long lead times), so that it cannot grow at once to meet the added demand?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-16: while their stock is fixed by earlier import orders, sellers have clearly fewer alternatives than rebate buyers, who can wait or keep their car.

question.text: While their supply is fixed, do the sellers have clearly fewer alternatives than the recipients (who can wait, buy something else or not buy at all)?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-12: some rebate buyers would otherwise have bought a non-eligible new model.

question.text: Would some recipients otherwise have bought one of the goods the payment does not cover (a non-eligible model, another form of the good)?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-8: some owners of failing cars can get a roadworthiness certificate for less than the rebate is worth to them.

question.text: For some who do not now meet the criteria, will changing what they do or own so as to meet them cost less than the payment is worth to them?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-9: importers and dealers have an existing association.

question.text: Can the sellers who gain from the payment organize to lobby for its extension or renewal at a cost below their stake (an existing trade association, a few large firms)?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-6: demand for rebates exceeds 120,000 at some point in the window (1.1 million eligible cars).

question.text: Will more people want the payment than its budget or number allows at some point while it is offered?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-5: buyers knew of the scheme from March and could delay purchases.

question.text: Could those who will be eligible put off a purchase they would otherwise make before the payment starts, until it does (the payment was announced in advance)?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-3: many window buyers would have bought a new car within the next few years anyway.

question.text: Would many of those who buy during the payment's window have bought the same good within the following few years anyway?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-20: buyers do not expect a repeat scheme (the opposite of A-15, p = 0.35); ministers have said there is no plan to repeat it.

question.text: Will the payment end when its window closes, rather than being renewed, extended or repeated soon after?

answer.rationale: No matching assumption in WE-019; judged from the text: new cars are imported against volumes ordered months ahead (shipping lead times), so at the end of the window import volumes set for the boom cannot be cut at once; WE-019 signs the post-window price fall (C-25) and calls it weak.

question.text: When the payment ends, will the sellers still be unable to cut their supply at once (stock already ordered, capacity built for the window)?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-4: the scrapped cars would otherwise have stayed in use (roadworthiness required; retirement at about 18 years).

question.text: Would the goods scrapped to obtain the payment otherwise have stayed in use for some years?

answer.rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-019 (illustrative figures), A-13: used-car imports cannot quickly replace the scrapped cars (25% duty and inspection).

question.text: Is other supply of used goods of this kind (imports, goods kept in use longer) unable to replace the scrapped ones quickly?

source_sentences: A private buyer who scraps an eligible old car receives a rebate of V$4,000 on a new car certified at 5.0 L/100 km or less, bought from a registered Vestrian dealer.
The rebate is paid by the Transport Ministry to the dealer and deducted on the invoice; one per buyer.
The old car must be 12 or more years old, registered to the buyer continuously since before 15 March, and hold a current roadworthiness certificate.
The budget is capped at V$480 million (120,000 rebates), first come, first served; the scheme closes early if the budget runs out.
It applies to purchase contracts signed from 1 July to 31 December of the same year and then expires.
Ministers have said there is no plan to repeat it, but have not ruled it out.
The government announced the rebate in its budget statement on 15 March.
The old car is delivered to a licensed dismantler, deregistered, and crushed within 30 days.
The rebate, the fees and the administration are funded by additional government bonds issued in the year, serviced and repaid from general revenue over 10 years.

context: About 200,000 new cars are sold in a normal year, roughly 40% of them models that use 5.0 liters of fuel per 100 km or less.
Of 4.5 million registered cars, about 1.1 million are 12 or more years old; a drivable car of that age typically sells for V$1,500 to V$5,000.
Used cars can be imported, but they pay a 25% duty and a registration inspection, so the used-car market runs mostly on the domestic fleet.
